grammar.name: The Hebrew Alphabet (א–ס), Vowels (Nikud), and Prefix Letters
grammar.explanation: Hebrew is written right-to-left, exactly like Arabic. The alphabet has 22 consonant letters; vowel marks (nikud) act like Arabic ḥarakāt. Letters א, ה, ו, י can double as long vowels (ḥurūf al-'illa). Five letters change shape at the end of a word (sofit), such as kaf (כ/ך), mem (מ/ם), and nun (נ/ן). Just like Arabic attached particles (بـ, الـ, وـ, لـ, من), single-letter prepositions and conjunctions attach directly to the next word: בְּ־ (in/at = بـ), הַ־ (the = الـ), וְ־ (and = وـ), לְ־ (to/for = لـ), and מִ־ (from = من). Bet (ב) sounds like /b/ with a dot (dagesh) and /v/ without.
grammar.pattern:
Prefixes: בְּ־ (in) / הַ־ (the) / וְ־ (and) + מִלָּה (word)
Sofit (endings): כ → ך | מ → ם | נ → ן
Nikud: ַ / ָ = /a/ | ֶ / ֵ = /e/ | ִ = /i/ | ֹ / וֹ = /o/ | ֻ / וּ = /u/

grammar.name: German Core Patterns: Capitalization, Genders & Verb Position
grammar.explanation: German differs from English in key ways: 1. All nouns are capitalized, whether at the start or in the middle of a sentence. 2. Every noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). 3. Special characters exist: the umlauts (ä, ö, ü) and the sharp 's' (ß). 4. German has no continuous tense (ich arbeite means both 'I work' and 'I am working'). 5. In main declarative clauses, the conjugated verb is always the second element.
grammar.pattern:
Nouns: CAPITALIZED (der Mann, die Frau, das Haus)
Genders: der (masc.) | die (fem.) | das (neut.)
Verb position 2: [Position 1] + [Verb] + [Subject/Rest...]
No continuous aspect: 'Ich lerne' = I learn / I am learning

grammar.name: Overview of the Hebrew Alphabet and Reading Basics
grammar.explanation: Hebrew is written from right to left. The alphabet consists of 22 consonants and no capital letters. Some letters have final forms (sofit) when they appear at the end of a word. grammar.name: Regular verbs in the present tense
grammar.explanation: To form the present tense of regular verbs in German, you take the infinitive (e.g., wohnen), remove the ending '-en' to find the stem ('wohn-'), and add the personal ending according to the subject. Remember that German has only one present tense that covers both simple and continuous aspects in English (e.g., 'ich wohne' = I live or I am living).
grammar.pattern:
ich: -e (komme)
du: -st (kommst)
er/sie/es/man: -t (kommt)
wir / sie / Sie: -en (kommen)
ihr: -t (kommt)

grammar.name: Final Letters (Otiyot Sofiyot) and Hard/Soft Pronunciation
grammar.explanation: Hebrew has five letters that change their shape when they appear at the very end of a word: ך (kaf), ם (mem), ן (nun), ף (pei), ץ (tzadi). Notice how ף (pei sofit) and ך (kaf sofit) at the end of words sound like /f/ and /ch/, similar to Arabic sound positions (ف and خ). Furthermore, letters like ב, כ, פ change pronunciation depending on a dot (dagesh): with a dot they are stop sounds (/b/, /k/, /p/), and without a dot they become fricatives (/v/, /ch/, /f/), perfectly mirroring Arabic letter developments.
grammar.pattern:
Regular -> Sofit: כ/ך, מ/ם, נ/ן, פ/ף, צ/ץ
פּ (/p/) -> פֹּה | פ (/f/) -> דַּף
כּ (/k/) -> כֹּפֶה | כ (/ch/) -> מִכְתָּב

grammar.name: Verb variations and irregular verbs (Präsens)
grammar.explanation: Most German verbs add standard endings to the stem, but some have spelling variations in the present tense, affecting du and er/sie/es. Stems ending in -d or -t (arbeiten) add an extra -e- before endings (du arbeitest, er arbeitet). Stems ending in -s, -ss, -ß, or -z (reisen, heißen) add only -t for du (du reist, du heißt). Irregular verbs change their stem vowel only for du and er/sie/es: a becomes ä (fahren → du fährst), e becomes i (treffen → du triffst; essen → du isst; nehmen → du nimmst), or e becomes ie (sehen → er sieht; lesen → er liest).
grammar.pattern:
arbeiten: du arbeitest, er arbeitet (-d/-t stem: +e-)
reisen: du reist, er reist (-s/-ß/-z stem: +t only)
a → ä: du fährst, er fährt (fahren, schlafen)
e → i/ie: du triffst, er liest (treffen, lesen)

grammar.name: Irregular verbs: haben and sein
grammar.explanation: In German, irregular verbs often change their stem vowel in the present tense for du and er/sie/es, such as in 'Der Freund isst einen Apfel' (essen -> isst). The verb haben drops the stem 'b' for du hast and er/sie/es hat, but stays regular for all other forms. The verb sein is completely irregular (ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, etc.) and must be learned by heart. Note that German has only one present tense: there is no continuous form like 'I am going'.
grammar.pattern:
haben: ich habe | du hast | er/sie/es hat | wir haben | ihr habt | sie/Sie haben
sein:  ich bin  | du bist | er/sie/es ist | wir sind  | ihr seid | sie/Sie sind

grammar.name: Separable Verbs in the Present Tense
grammar.explanation: Separable verbs consist of a prefix and a main verb (e.g., auf + stehen). In present tense main clauses, the main verb stays in second position and conjugates normally, while the split-off prefix moves to the very end of the clause. In sentences with two main clauses, each prefix goes to the end of its respective clause. Common separable prefixes include ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, and zu-. Note that prefixes like be-, er-, ge-, and ver- are inseparable and remain attached to the verb.
grammar.pattern:
Position 2: Main verb  |  End of clause: Prefix
Subject + [Conjugated Verb] + ... + [Prefix].
Jens + steht + um halb acht Uhr + auf.
Clause 1 [Verb ... Prefix 1], und / aber Clause 2 [Verb ... Prefix 2].

examples.de: Nico steht um fünf Uhr morgens auf.
examples.en: Nico gets up at five o'clock in the morning.
He goes shopping in the supermarket.

examples.de: Die Kinder sehen nicht viel fern.
examples.en: The children don't watch much television.

examples.de: Herr Schuster schläft erst um Mitternacht ein, aber er steht schon um fünf Uhr auf.
examples.en: Mr Schuster only falls asleep at midnight, but he gets up at five o'clock.

text.title: Jens Fischers Tag
text.de: Jens schaltet den Wecker um sieben Uhr aus. Er steht um halb acht Uhr auf. Er fängt seine Arbeit um neun Uhr an. Mittags ruft er seine Freundin an. Am Nachmittag druckt er viele Dokumente aus. Um siebzehn Uhr hört er mit seiner Arbeit auf. Nach der Arbeit kauft er im Supermarkt ein. Abends sieht er manchmal fern. Er schläft meistens nach Mitternacht ein.
text.en_gist: Jens Fischer goes through his daily schedule from waking up in the morning to falling asleep after midnight.

phrases.de: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.
phrases.en: I get up at six o'clock.

phrases.de: Er kauft nach der Arbeit im Supermarkt ein.
phrases.en: He goes shopping in the supermarket after work.

phrases.de: Abends sieht er fern und schläft spät ein.
phrases.en: In the evening he watches television and falls asleep late.

lesson.exam_tip: When reading short texts or emails in the exam, always scan to the very end of the sentence. A separable prefix at the end (like 'ein' in 'kauft ... ein') changes the core meaning of the verb!

unit.title: The imperative
unit.objective: give instructions and make requests with du, ihr and Sie
unit.book: Basic German, unit 6: Imperatives (pp. 39–44)

lesson.title: Der Imperativ
lesson.goal: Give instructions and make requests using du, ihr, and Sie.

grammar.name: The Imperative (du, ihr, Sie)
grammar.explanation: Separable verbs split off their prefix and place it at the end of the sentence. For example, Nico steht um fünf Uhr morgens auf. The imperative gives commands with the verb in first position. For 'du', drop the ending -en and pronoun (Komm!); add -e for stems ending in -d/-t (Warte!), keep e->i stem changes (Sprich!), but drop a->ä umlauts (Fahr!). For 'ihr', add -t to the stem without pronoun (Kommt!). For formal 'Sie', use the infinitive followed by Sie (Kommen Sie!). Separable prefixes go to the end (Fang an!). Irregular 'sein' uses Sei!, Seid!, and Seien Sie!.
grammar.pattern:
du: Stem (+ -e) | Lies! / Warte! / Fang ... an!
ihr: Stem + -t | Lest! / Wartet! / Fangt ... an!
Sie: Infinitive + Sie | Lesen Sie! / Warten Sie! / Fangen Sie an!
sein: Sei! (du) | Seid! (ihr) | Seien Sie! (Sie)

examples.en: Come (here)!
Speak quietly!
Start!
Be careful!

text.title: Anweisungen im Büro
text.de: Kommen Sie bitte herein! Warten Sie bitte noch fünf Minuten. Herr Kurz, öffnen Sie das Fenster und bringen Sie mir einen Saft. Fangen Sie dann an! Haben Sie ein bisschen Geduld und seien Sie vorsichtig. Fahr rechts, Nico! Sprich leise und lies die SMS!
text.en_gist: A person gives various polite instructions and commands to colleagues in an office setting.

lesson.exam_tip: In Hören audio tasks (announcements and messages), listen for the verb at the very beginning of the sentence to quickly spot instructions and requests.

unit.title: Asking questions
unit.objective: ask yes/no and W-questions with correct word order
unit.book: Basic German, unit 7: Questions (pp. 45–50)

lesson.title: Fragen stellen: W-Fragen und Ja/Nein-Fragen
lesson.goal: Ask yes/no and W-questions using correct German word order in both formal and informal contexts.

grammar.name: W-Questions and Yes/No Questions
grammar.explanation: In the last unit, we learned that imperatives give direct commands, like 'Fahr mehr mit dem Fahrrad!' for du or 'Warten Sie bitte!' for Sie. Remember to drop verb endings for informal commands and place the verb first for formal commands. In this unit, we form questions. W-questions start with a question word (wer, was, wo, woher, wohin, wie, wann) in position 1, followed by the verb in position 2, then the subject. Yes/no questions move the finite verb directly to position 1, with the subject right after. Use 'wie' for names, addresses, and time. German does not use the auxiliary 'do'.
grammar.pattern:
W-Question: Question Word + Verb + Subject + ...?
(z.B. Wo wohnt er? / Wie ist Ihre E-Mail-Adresse?)
Yes/No Question: Verb + Subject + ...?
(z.B. Sprechen Sie Deutsch? / Kommt Timo wirklich aus Bremen?)

examples.en: Where do you come from?
What is your address?
Do you stay in the hotel 'Zur Sonne'?
Does Timo really come from Bremen?

text.title: Ein Interview mit Oliver Gehrs
text.de:
– Wie ist Ihr Name?
– Mein Name ist Oliver Gehrs.
– Was sind Sie von Beruf?
– Ich bin Journalist.
– Wann beginnt Ihre Arbeit?
– Meine Arbeit beginnt meistens um 8.00 Uhr.
– Ist die Arbeit interessant?
– Ja, die Arbeit ist sehr interessant.
– Haben Sie Kinder?
– Ja, ich habe eine Tochter und zwei Söhne.
– Sprechen Sie Spanisch?
– Nein, ich spreche kein Spanisch, aber ich spreche sehr gut Englisch.
text.en_gist: Oliver Gehrs answers interview questions about his name, profession as a journalist, working hours, family, and language skills.

phrases.de: Fährt der Zug um acht Uhr ab?
phrases.en: Does the train depart at eight o'clock?
Are you really coming on Sunday?

lesson.exam_tip: When writing short SMS messages or emails for Goethe A1, ensure your questions start with either a W-word or a verb—never put the subject first in a question. Pay close attention to spelling common words accurately (e.g., 'wohnt' with 'o', and neuter nouns like 'das Museum' and 'das Jahr').

unit.title: Articles
unit.objective: use definite, indefinite and negative articles (der, ein, kein)
unit.book: Basic German, unit 8: Articles (pp. 51–56)

lesson.title: Nomen und Artikel
lesson.goal: The learner can correctly use definite and indefinite articles (der, die, das, ein, eine) to refer to specific and unspecific nouns in German.

grammar.name: Definite and Indefinite Articles
grammar.explanation: To ask questions in German, place the verb first for yes/no questions or after the question word. Ensure correct subject-verb agreement, for example: Der Mann und die Frau haben Zeit. Definite articles (der, die, das, plural die) refer to specific nouns. Indefinite articles (ein, eine, ein) refer to unspecific nouns and have no plural form. Definite articles are required with seasons (der Sommer), certain countries (die Schweiz), street names, and abstract nouns (das Leben), but omitted for playing instruments. Indefinite articles are omitted for occupations and nationalities unless an adjective is present (ein guter Rechtsanwalt). Das or dies functions as 'this/that is' or 'these/those are'.
grammar.pattern:
Masc: der / ein Mann
Fem:  die / eine Frau
Neut: das / ein Kind
Plur: die / --- Kinder
Demo: Das/Dies ist... | Das/Dies sind...

examples.en: The man is called Nicolai.

examples.de: Eine Frau aus Leipzig wohnt hier.
examples.en: A woman from Leipzig lives here.
Leon is a good lawyer.
This is the Brandenburg Gate.

text.title: Menschen und Ideen
text.de: Der Mann heißt Nicolai. Er trinkt Kaffee. Seine Frau kommt aus Leipzig. Sie hat eine gute Idee. Das Kind ist fünf Jahre alt und braucht ein neues Computerspiel. Der Sommer war schön. Ist das die Goethestraße? Das ist der Manager und das sind die Spieler. Das Leben ist schön!
text.en_gist: A short overview describing people, their origins, activities, and surroundings using definite and indefinite articles.

phrases.de: Ich möchte ein Bier und eine Cola, bitte.
phrases.en: I would like a beer and a cola, please.

lesson.exam_tip: In the Reading section (Lesen Teil 1–4), pay close attention to articles (der, die, das, ein, eine) in short notices and signs to determine whether a text refers to a specific place/item or just any general object.

unit.title: Nouns and gender
unit.objective: predict a noun's gender from its ending and learn nouns with their article
unit.book: Basic German, unit 9: Nouns and gender (pp. 57–63)

lesson.title: Nomen und Genus
lesson.goal: Predict a noun's gender from its ending or category and learn nouns with their articles.

grammar.name: Nouns and Gender (Nomen und Genus)
grammar.explanation: German uses three definite articles for singular nouns: der (masculine), die (feminine), and das (neuter), which all become die in the plural. Correctly identifying these articles is essential because they show grammatical gender. In German, gender can often be predicted by word endings or semantic categories. Nouns ending in -ig, -ismus, -ling, -or (and days, seasons, car makes) are masculine (der). Nouns ending in -ei, -heit, -keit, -ung, -schaft, -tät, -ie, -ik, -ion (and female persons, trees, flowers) are feminine (die). Nouns ending in -chen, -lein, -ma, -ment, -o, -um (and young persons, metals, hotels) are neuter (das). In compound nouns, the final noun always determines the gender of the entire word. Remember: all German nouns are capitalized!
grammar.pattern:
der (masculine): -ig, -ismus, -ling, -or | days, seasons, cars
die (feminine): -ei, -heit, -keit, -ung, -schaft, -tät | female persons
das (neuter): -chen, -lein, -ma, -ment, -o, -um | young persons
Compound: die Reise + der Pass -> der Reisepass

examples.de: Der Tisch und das Regal sind kaputt.
examples.en: The table and the shelf are broken.
The bakery sells a newspaper.
The girl works in the office.

examples.de: Die Reise plus der Pass ist der Reisepass.
examples.en: The trip plus the pass equals the passport.

text.title: Eine Woche in Berlin
text.de: Berlin ist eine fantastische Stadt. Das Hotel Hilton liegt sehr zentral. Der Service ist ausgezeichnet und das Essen im Restaurant ist sehr gut. Die Woche geht so schnell vorbei. Die Menschen in Berlin sind sehr freundlich. Heute Abend gehen wir zuerst in ein Konzert und feiern unseren letzten Tag.
text.en_gist: A visitor describes a wonderful stay at a central hotel in Berlin, enjoying the food, friendly people, and final evening concert.

phrases.de: Achtung an Gleis 1: Wann kommt der Zug an?
phrases.en: Attention at platform 1: When does the train arrive?

phrases.de: Die U-Bahn fährt direkt zum Stadtzentrum.
phrases.en: The underground train goes directly to the city center.

phrases.de: Das Restaurant im Hotel Hilton ist heute geöffnet.
phrases.en: The restaurant in the Hilton hotel is open today.

phrases.de: Bitte halten Sie Ihren Reisepass bereit.

lesson.exam_tip: In the Hören (listening) section, use the reading time before audio plays to highlight nouns and their articles. Knowing a noun's gender helps you spot keywords in train announcements or phone messages faster.

unit.title: Plural of nouns
unit.objective: form the plural of the main noun groups
unit.book: Basic German, unit 10: Plural of nouns (pp. 64–70)

lesson.title: Plural der Nomen
lesson.goal: Form the plural of the main German noun groups accurately across masculine, feminine, neuter, and foreign nouns.

grammar.name: Plural of Nouns (Plural der Nomen)
grammar.explanation: In German, every noun has a specific gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). Learning a noun with its gender is essential because gender indicates how its plural is formed. German uses several plural patterns: most masculine nouns add -e or -¨e; about 90% of feminine nouns add -n or -en; neuter nouns commonly add -e or -¨er. Nouns ending in -er, -el, -en, -chen, or -lein take no ending (sometimes adding an umlaut). Imported foreign words from English or French usually take -s.
grammar.pattern:
m: +e / +¨e (der Tag -> die Tage, der Zug -> die Züge)
f: +n / +en / +¨e (die Tasse -> die Tassen, die Stadt -> die Städte)
n: +e / +¨er (das Jahr -> die Jahre, das Buch -> die Bücher)
Foreign: +s (das Handy -> die Handys)
-er/-el/-en/-chen/-lein: no ending / +¨ (das Zimmer -> die Zimmer, der Apfel -> die Äpfel)

examples.de: Ich hätte gern zwei Flaschen, bitte.
examples.en: I would like two bottles, please.
The house has four rooms.
She reads three newspapers.
He has three mobile phones.

text.title: Eine kurze E-Mail an einen Freund
text.de: Hallo! Das Haus hier ist sehr schön. Es hat vier Zimmer. Auf dem Tisch liegen drei Bücher und zwei Zeitungen. Am Wochenende esse ich Äpfel und trinke Tee aus zwei Tassen. Gehst du heute auf zwei Partys?
text.en_gist: A short message describing a nice house with four rooms, books, newspapers, and asking about weekend plans.

phrases.de: Ich hätte gern zwei Flaschen, bitte.
phrases.en: I would like two bottles, please.
At the weekend I sleep in.
Are we going to two parties?

lesson.exam_tip: In the A1 writing exam (SMS or short E-Mail), ensure correct plural endings for common items (e.g. zwei Flaschen, drei Zimmer). Note that English loanwords ending in -y just take -s in German (Partys, Hobbys, not Parties). Always remember verb position: after time phrases like 'Am Wochenende', the verb comes second (Am Wochenende esse ich...).

unit.title: The four cases
unit.objective: explain what the four cases do in a sentence
unit.book: Basic German, unit 11: The four cases (pp. 71–76)

lesson.title: Die vier Fälle
lesson.goal: The learner can explain what the four cases do in a sentence and name the three determining factors.

grammar.name: The four cases
grammar.explanation: Remember from our last unit that nouns change their plural forms to show more than one. In German, nouns also play different roles in a sentence, which are signalled by cases that change the endings of accompanying words like articles. There are four cases. The nominative is used for the subject (the agent doing the action). The accusative is for the direct object (the receiver of the action). The dative is for the indirect object (to or for whom the action is done). The genitive shows possession or a relationship between two nouns. Case is determined by three factors: the role of the noun in the sentence, the verb, and prepositions.
grammar.pattern:
Nominative: Subject (Der Mann liest.)
Accusative: Direct Object (den Roman)
Dative: Indirect Object (dem Freund)
Genitive: Possession (des Mannes)

examples.en: The man is reading.
The man is reading the novel.

examples.de: Der Mann gibt dem Freund einen Roman.
examples.en: The man gives the friend a novel.
The man's hat.

text.title: Die vier Fälle im Satz
text.de: Der Mann liest einen Roman. Er gibt dem Freund ein Geschenk. Das ist der Hut des Mannes.
text.en_gist: A short text illustrating the nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive cases in action.

lesson.exam_tip: When speaking and planning together, listen carefully to verbs and prepositions as they dictate whether you need the accusative or dative case.

unit.title: The nominative
unit.objective: identify the subject and use the nominative correctly
unit.book: Basic German, unit 12: The nominative case (pp. 77–79)

lesson.title: Der Nominativ: Das Subjekt im Satz
lesson.goal: Identify the subject of a sentence and use nominative determiners correctly.

grammar.name: The Nominative Case (Der Nominativ)
grammar.explanation: German nouns change according to their case, which depends on the role of the noun in the sentence, the verb, and prepositions. These four cases alter articles and endings to show who or what performs or receives an action. German uses the nominative case when the noun is the subject—the person or thing doing the action. You also use the nominative after the verbs sein ('to be') and werden ('to become'). Determiners, such as der Artikel (definite articles), indefinite articles, possessives, and negative kein, take specific nominative forms. To spot the subject, ask 'who or what is doing the action?'; remember that the subject does not have to be at the beginning of the sentence.
grammar.pattern:
masculine: der / ein / mein / kein Mann
feminine: die / eine / meine / keine Frau
neuter: das / ein / mein / kein Kind
plural: die / — / meine / keine Gäste
Special verbs: [Subject] + sein / werden + [Nominative]

examples.en: The man is listening to music.
The woman reads the magazine.
He is an interesting man.

examples.de: Morgen fährt die Klasse nach Berlin.
examples.en: Tomorrow the class is going to Berlin.

text.title: Der Nominativ im Alltag
text.de: Der Mann hört Musik. Die Frau liest das Magazin und das Kind kauft einen Keks. Die Gäste wollen es nicht. Er ist ein interessanter Mann und der Wagen ist ein BMW. Es wird ein schöner Tag. Er ist Ingenieur und sie wird Sportlehrerin. Morgen fährt die Klasse nach Berlin. Zum Frühstück trinkt er grünen Tee. Wer macht die Aktion? Die Klasse fährt und er trinkt Tee.
text.en_gist: The text demonstrates subjects performing actions and nouns standing in the nominative case, including after the verbs sein and werden.

phrases.de: Wer oder was macht die Aktion?
phrases.en: Who or what is doing the action?
It's going to be a nice day.
The newspaper is called Die Welt.

lesson.exam_tip: When reading short texts or ads for Lesen Teil 1–4, identify the main verb first and ask 'who or what?' to instantly spot the subject in the nominative case, even if it appears after the verb.

unit.title: The accusative
unit.objective: use the accusative for direct objects and after accusative prepositions
unit.book: Basic German, unit 13: The accusative case (pp. 80–84)

lesson.title: Der Akkusativ
lesson.goal: The learner will be able to use the accusative case for direct objects and after accusative prepositions.

grammar.name: The accusative case (Der Akkusativ)
grammar.explanation: The nominative case marks the subject performing the action (der, die, das; ein, eine, ein). It shows who or what is doing something in the sentence. In contrast, the accusative case marks the direct object (the receiver of the action) and follows specific prepositions: bis, durch, für, gegen, ohne, um. Only masculine determiners change ending in the accusative: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen (e.g., einen Regenschirm, not ein). Neuter (das/ein), feminine (die/eine), and plural forms remain identical to the nominative.
grammar.pattern:
masculine: der -> den | ein -> einen | mein -> meinen
feminine:  die -> die | eine -> eine  | meine -> meine
neuter:    das -> das | ein -> ein    | mein -> mein
plural:    die -> die | —             | meine -> meine
prepositions + Akk: bis, durch, für, gegen, ohne, um

examples.en: I've got an umbrella.

examples.de: Wir fahren gerade durch einen Tunnel.
examples.en: We are just driving through a tunnel.

examples.de: Das Buch ist für einen Freund.
examples.en: The book is for a friend.
She is coming without her boyfriend.

text.title: Dinge für die neue Wohnung
text.de: Ich brauche einen Küchentisch, einen Kühlschrank und eine Kaffeemaschine. Mein Bruder kauft den Computer und einen Regenschirm. Wir fahren mit dem Auto durch einen Tunnel. Er trägt einen Anzug ohne eine Krawatte. Das Kochbuch ist für meine Schwester.
text.en_gist: The speaker lists items needed for a new apartment and describes purchases made for family members.

phrases.de: Das Buch ist für meinen Vater.
phrases.en: The book is for my father.
We are driving through the tunnel.

lesson.exam_tip: In listening tasks (Durchsagen & Telefonnachrichten), listen specifically for the '-en' ending (einen, den, meinen) to identify masculine direct objects or nouns following prepositions like für and ohne.

unit.title: The dative
unit.objective: use the dative for indirect objects and after dative prepositions
unit.book: Basic German, unit 14: The dative case (pp. 85–89)

lesson.title: Der Dativ: Indirekte Objekte und Präpositionen
lesson.goal: Use the dative case correctly for indirect objects, dative verbs, and after dative prepositions.

grammar.name: The Dative Case (Der Dativ)
grammar.explanation: The accusative case marks the direct object, changing masculine articles like der Supermarkt to den Supermarkt. It shows who or what directly receives an action. The dative case is used for indirect objects—the person or thing to or for whom something is done. Masculine and neuter determiners take -em (dem/einem/meinem), feminine takes -er (der/einer/meiner), and plural takes -en (den/meinen), usually adding -n to the plural noun (den Gästen). Dative is also required after verbs such as antworten, begegnen, helfen, danken, gehören, gratulieren, folgen, trauen, and prepositions like aus, außer, bei, gegenüber, mit, nach, seit, von, zu.
grammar.pattern:
Masc/Neut: dem / einem / meinem (-em)
Fem: der / einer / meiner (-er)
Plural: den / meinen (-en) + Noun-n
Prepositions: aus, außer, bei, gegenüber, mit, nach, seit, von, zu

examples.de: Sie schickt dem Mann eine SMS.
examples.en: She sends the man a text message.

examples.de: Lara hilft ihrer Tochter mit den Hausaufgaben.
examples.en: Lara helps her daughter with the homework.

examples.de: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Bus.
examples.en: I go by bus every day.
He comes from Turkey.

text.title: Geschenke für die Gastfamilie
text.de: Maria gibt ihrer Gastfamilie viele Geschenke. Sie gibt der Großmutter eine Schachtel Pralinen und dem Großvater ein Buch über Nelson Mandela. Der Mutter gibt sie einen Strauß Blumen und dem Vater eine Flasche Wein. Tim zeigt den Gästen die Umgebung. Nach der Arbeit fährt Maria mit dem Bus zu meiner Freundin.
text.en_gist: Maria gives presents to her host family, and Tim shows the guests around before Maria visits a friend after work.

phrases.de: Sie gibt der Großmutter eine Schachtel Pralinen.
phrases.en: She gives the grandmother a box of chocolates.

phrases.de: Ich helfe dir mit den Hausaufgaben.
phrases.en: I'm helping you with the homework.

phrases.de: Nach der Arbeit gehe ich einkaufen.

phrases.en: We'll go to my girlfriend's place.

lesson.exam_tip: When writing a short SMS (20–30 words) or E-Mail (30–40 words) for the exam, double-check your prepositional phrases. Prepositions like 'mit', 'nach', and 'zu' always trigger the dative: use 'mit dem Bus' (masculine/neuter -em) or 'zu meiner Freundin' (feminine -er), not accusative forms like 'den' or English possessives like 'his sister' when you mean 'my sister' (meiner Schwester).

unit.title: The genitive
unit.objective: recognise and use the genitive for possession
unit.book: Basic German, unit 15: The genitive case (pp. 90–93)

lesson.title: Der Genitiv (The Genitive Case)
lesson.goal: Recognise and use the genitive case to indicate possession.

grammar.name: The Genitive Case
grammar.explanation: In the dative case, articles change to show indirect objects or locations (e.g., dem, der, den). Plural dative nouns also add an extra -n. The genitive case shows possession and usually follows the main noun. Determiners for masculine and neuter end in -es, while feminine and plural end in -er. One-syllable masculine/neuter nouns add -es (des Mannes), and longer ones add -s (des Computers). Names add an -s without an apostrophe (Hannahs Scooter). In spoken German, von + dative often replaces the genitive.
grammar.pattern:
Masc/Neut: des/meines Mannes (-es/-s ending on noun)
Fem/Plural: der/meiner Frau (no noun ending)
Names: Hannahs Scooter (no apostrophe)
Spoken alternative: von + Dative (das Auto von meinem Bruder)

examples.de: Das ist die Tasche meines Vaters.
examples.en: That is my father's bag.

examples.de: Das ist das Auto meiner Tante.
examples.en: That is my aunt's car.

examples.de: Das ist das Spielzeug meines Kindes.
examples.en: That is my child's toy.
This is Hannah's scooter.

text.title: Die Sachen meiner Familie
text.de: Das ist die Tasche meines Vaters und da steht das Auto meiner Tante. Wo ist das Spielzeug meines Kindes? Hier steht auch der Scooter meiner Schwester. Die Meinung meiner Freunde ist klar: Das Auto von meinem Bruder ist sehr alt!
text.en_gist: A person describes items belonging to family members and friends using the genitive case.

phrases.de: Wie ist der Name Ihres Vaters?
Das ist das Auto meines Bruders.
Das sind die Sportsachen meiner Frau.
phrases.en: These are my wife's sports items.

phrases.de: Das ist der Computer meiner Chefin.

lesson.exam_tip: In the speaking exam ('Sprechen: Über sich erzählen'), use the genitive to show precise language skills when introducing your family or possessions. If you hesitate on genitive endings during spoken interaction, using 'von' + dative is also widely accepted.

unit.title: The vowels (nikud)
unit.objective: read words with nikud: the vowel marks, shva, semi-vowels and stress
unit.book: Routledge Hebrew, The vowels (nikud) and the syllable (pp. 33–36)

lesson.title: הַתְּנוּעוֹת וְהַנִּקּוּד
lesson.goal: Read Hebrew words accurately using vowel marks (nikud), identify shva and semi-vowels, apply furtive patach, and place word stress correctly.

grammar.name: Nikud, Furtive Patach, and Word Stress
grammar.explanation: Hebrew has 5 vowel sounds (/a, e, i, o, u/) written with points called נִקּוּד. The שְׁוָא (ְ) acts either as zero vowel (like Arabic سُكُون, e.g. שְׁמִי /shmi/) or a quick /e/. Guttural letters (א, ה, ח, ע) take semi-vowels (חֲטָפִים). When a word ends in guttural ח or ע preceded by an /i, e, o, u/ vowel, a 'furtive patach' (פַּתַח גְּנוּבָה) slips in: read the /a/ sound BEFORE the final consonant (לוּחַ is /lu-ach/, not /lu-cha/). Modern Hebrew stress falls on either the ultimate syllable (מִלְּרַע, e.g. שָׁבוּעַ, תַּרְגִּיל) or penultimate syllable (מִלְּעֵיל, e.g. לַיְלָה, מֶלֶךְ).
grammar.pattern:
Vowels: /a/ (ַ, ָ) | /e/ (ֶ, ֵ) | /i/ (ִ) | /o/ (ֹ, וֹ) | /u/ (ֻ, וּ)
Shva nach (ְ) = سكون (silent) vs. Shva na (ְ) = short /e/
Furtive Patach: [Vowel ≠ a] + [חַ / עַ] -> pronounce /...ach/, /...a'/
Stress: Last syllable (מִלְּרַע) or 2nd-to-last (מִלְּעֵיל)

grammar.name: Personal pronouns (Personalpronomen)
grammar.explanation: In the previous unit, we covered the genitive case, which indicates possession or relationship (e.g., das Haus meines Nachbarn). Remember that masculine/neuter nouns add -s/-es while feminine/plural take der. In this unit, personal pronouns replace nouns and change according to grammatical gender and case. Nominative pronouns act as the subject (ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie). Accusative pronouns replace direct objects or follow prepositions like für and ohne (mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie/Sie). Dative pronouns replace indirect objects or follow prepositions like bei, mit, zu and verbs like helfen (mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen/Ihnen). Neuter nouns like das Kind take es (Acc) and ihm (Dat). The pronoun man refers to people generally.
grammar.pattern:
Nom: ich | du | er / sie / es | wir | ihr | sie / Sie
Acc: mich | dich | ihn / sie / es | uns | euch | sie / Sie
Dat: mir | dir | ihm / ihr / ihm | uns | euch | ihnen / Ihnen

grammar.name: The Nikud System, Syllables, Furtive Patach, and Stress
grammar.explanation: Last unit introduced the 22 letters of the Alef-Bet and their consonant sounds. Hebrew is written primarily with consonants, while vowel sounds are added using a system of dots and dashes called Nikud (נִקּוּד). Modern Hebrew has 5 vowel sounds (/a/, /e/, /i/, /o/, /u/). A Shva (שְׁוָוא) indicates either no vowel sound or a short /e/. Guttural letters (א, ה, ח, ע) take semi-vowels (Chataf). In Ktiv Male, letters like ו and י act as vowels. Syllables are either open (ending in a vowel letter) or closed. When a word ends in a guttural letter (ח or ע) preceded by a non-/a/ vowel, an extra 'Furtive Patach' (פַּתַּח גְּנוּבָה) is added under it and pronounced BEFORE the consonant sound (e.g., רֵיחַ = rei-ach, שָׁבוּעַ = sha-vu-a). Stress is usually on the final or penult syllable.
grammar.pattern:
Vowel marks: /a/ (ַ, ָ), /e/ (ֶ, ֵ), /i/ (ִ), /o/ (ֹ, ֹו), /u/ (ֻ, ּו)
Shva: ְ (silent or /e/ at start/consecutive)
Furtive Patach: [vowel ≠ /a/] + ח/ע + ַ  ➔ pronounced /...aCH/ or /...aA/
Stress: Last syllable (מִלְרַע) or Next-to-last (מִלְעֵיל)
